title: Reading a pauri of Bhai Gurdas
hookLine: a slow reading of one pauri, its picture, its point

cards: A forest. Tall trees, thick undergrowth, a bamboo grove rattling in the wind. And somewhere in the middle, one sandalwood tree.
That's the whole opening of today's stanza. No hero, no journey, no miracle, just trees standing next to each other. For days we've heard about Bhai Gurdas and his vars.
Today we stop talking about him and read him slowly, the way a ragi or a katha teacher would. Today: pauri.

teach.b: A pauri is one stanza of a var, and Bhai Gurdas often builds his around a picture you could find in any village. Read it in three steps. Step one: the picture.
Let it stand before you look for meaning. A sandalwood tree grows in the forest, its fragrance spreads, and the ordinary trees around it pick up the scent. Stay with that.

teach.h: STEP TWO: THE BAMBOO THAT STAYS THE SAME.
teach.b: Bhai Gurdas pictures one tree that doesn't take the scent: the bamboo, standing right beside the sandalwood, tall and hollow.
Some readers hear pride in it, so taken up with its own height that the fragrance never gets in. Now the picture has tension. Closeness alone didn't change it.

teach.h: STEP THREE: THE POINT, THE SANGAT.
LET THE PICTURE MAKE THE POINT.
teach.b: For Bhai Gurdas, the sandalwood is the Guru, or the company of the Guru's Sikhs, the sangat. Ordinary people sitting near it take on something of its fragrance.
But a person can sit right beside it, every week, and stay exactly the same, if they're hollow and puffed up with themselves. The pauri doesn't scold. It shows you the bamboo and lets you notice it.
That's the method: one picture, held long enough to see it; one twist that gives it an edge; one point, which the picture has already made before anyone states it.

how: In katha, a teacher in the gurdwara takes one pauri of Bhai Gurdas, describes its picture, and draws out its point for the sangat, often alongside a line of Gurbani.

the refrain sung between the verses of a hymn

games.q: inside the pauri — tap the pairs.

s: standing close to the sandalwood is enough to change you
the bamboo stands right beside it and stays the same.
Bhai Gurdas builds this pauri around a picture from the forest
a sandalwood tree, ordinary trees, and a bamboo.

games.q: a sandalwood tree grows in the forest, and its scent spreads. which tree stays without the fragrance?
games.why: in the pauri, it's the bamboo, right beside the sandalwood, hollow and tall, that never takes the scent.

practice: Close your eyes and build the picture first: the forest, the sandalwood, the ordinary trees slowly taking on its scent, and stay with it without asking what it means.

Then bring in the bamboo, tall and hollow, right beside it, and only near the end let the point arrive: where in your life are you sitting close to something good? If you pray, you can say Waheguru softly at the end.

wordCard.voice: Pauri, one stanza of a var, read first for its picture, then its twist, then the point that comes out of the picture itself.

carryVoice: Your line: one picture, one point. In this pauri, the sandalwood does all the talking. Until tomorrow.
